evidence_quotes.quote: In this study, we examine how technocratic insulation, different ways of knowing (WoKs), and participatory governance shape long-term resilience in one of Brazil’s most important river basins, the Piracicaba-Capivari-Jundiaí (PCJ).

This paper examines how diﬀerent WoKs held by Brazilian water managers, combined with the historical hierarchies of diﬀerent types of technical expertise, contribute to perpetuating a technocratic governance model to address water challenges.

Based on 27 in-depth interviews with members of the PCJ River Basin Committees, we show how a distinct preference for infrastructure-based solutions to deal with on-going and upcoming challenges may be unsustainable under climate change

We collected information about Committee members’ perceptions of the planning process and governance priorities through in-depth semi-structured interviews with members of the PCJ Committees and Technical Chambers between September to December 2018.

Rather, many members of the PCJ Committees look toward the construction of large new reservoirs, an inter-basin water transfer system, more sophisticated water treatment plants, and water loss reduction programs as the main avenues to increasing water security.

criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access. This is a river-basin water-resources management and climate-adaptation planning study (Exclusion Criterion 7) focusing on how members of the Piracicaba-Capivari-Jundiaí (PCJ) River Basin Committees frame water security and prioritize bulk gray infrastructure (reservoirs, inter-basin transfers) versus nature-based watershed restoration. Mentions of sanitation access and 2014–2015 rationing appear only as historical/contextual background.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/literal broad wording of Criterion 2 because it examines water governance and institutional factors—specifically technocratic insulation, power asymmetries, and epistemic 'ways of knowing' (WoKs) in participatory river basin committees under Brazil's 1997 Water Law. However, it FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because epistemic framings and technocratic dominance in basin-wide resource planning are macro-governance/planning processes rather than a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure rules, tariffs, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure governing access). Overall plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper also fails Criteria 1 and 4.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative case study combining primary semi-structured interviews (n = 27 PCJ Committee and Technical Chamber members), participant observation of committee and technical group meetings (2014–2016 and October–December 2018), media content coding, and documentary review of state and basin water plans.
criterion_notes.c4: No outcome relevant to household or community service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is measured or reported. Reported outcomes are committee members' problem framings, preferred basin-level planning strategies (gray reservoir/transfer infrastructure vs. green infrastructure/stream restoration in Plano de Bacias), and qualitative assessments of institutional path-dependence and adaptive capacity.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (PCJ River Basin Committees and active committee members, n = 27 interviewees), exposure/analytical factor (technocratic dominance and engineering vs. environmental Ways of Knowing), governance/planning outcome, and qualitative case-study design are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative case study (semi-structured interviews, participant observation, media coding, and documentary analysis)
population_and_sample: Piracicaba-Capivari-Jundiaí (PCJ) River Basin Committees and Technical Chambers in Brazil (600 total members; 27 active members interviewed: 14 water users, 5 government representatives, 4 civil-society representatives, and 4 unaffiliated members; plus participant observation of meetings in 2014–2016 and October–December 2018)
exposure: Technocratic dominance / insulation and decision-makers' epistemic 'ways of knowing' (WoKs: engineering/IWRM approach vs. environmental/adaptive management approach) in participatory river basin governance
outcome: Basin-level water resource planning priorities and preferred adaptation strategies (preference for gray infrastructure such as reservoirs and inter-basin water transfers vs. green infrastructure / nature-based watershed restoration) and qualitative implications for long-term basin resilience
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; cf. Exclusion Criterion 7, water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Although this is an empirical qualitative study of water governance in Brazil's PCJ River Basin Committees, it investigates how technocratic dominance and epistemic 'ways of knowing' (engineering vs. environmental framings) shape basin-scale resource planning preferences (new reservoirs and inter-basin transfers vs. nature-based watershed restoration) for climate resilience. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no), does not analyze a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (c2 = no, though it satisfies the plain governance wording of Criterion 2), and reports no household/community service-access outcome (c4 = no). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded due to failing Criteria 1 and 4.
